articles_hidden.title: Mechanism of catalytic regulation by an allosteric hot spot in dihydrofolate reductase
articles_hidden.authors: Paul Guénon, Marion Chauveau, Karolina Filipowska, Iñaki Tuñón, Clément Nizak, Kimberly A. Reynolds, Guillaume Stirnemann, Olivier Rivoire, Damien Laage
articles_hidden.abstract: Allostery is central to catalysis and regulation, yet how distal perturbations control enzyme activity remains unresolved. Here we elucidate how a distal allosteric hot spot regulates catalysis in dihydrofolate reductase, a benchmark enzyme exhibiting latent allostery. We combine enhanced conformational sampling, reactive free-energy calculations of the chemical step, and perturbation-induced nonequilibrium molecular dynamics with evolutionary analysis and experimental kinetics to obtain a comprehensive molecular description of conformational landscapes, catalytic activity, and allosteric communication. We show that a mutational perturbation at the hot spot redistributes the populations of two globally similar conformations with a subtle but critical structural difference that makes one catalytically competent and the other not. Nonequilibrium relaxation simulations further reveal that the transition between these two states in the mutant proceeds through a stepwise sequence of local structural rearrangements rather than a concerted global motion. Guided by this mechanism, we rationally engineer a compensatory second-site mutation that partially restores activity. These results provide a unified thermodynamic and kinetic view of allostery and establish a general, mechanistically guided framework for engineering allosteric regulation in enzymes.

articles_hidden.title: A causal account of the neural origins of mental fatigue
articles_hidden.authors: Hongmei Xia, Gizem Vural, Antonia Susnjar, Helge J. Zöllner, Rebekka S. Mattes, Alexander Soutschek
articles_hidden.abstract: Successful goal-directed behavior often requires the exertion of effortful cognitive control processes, but it remains unclear why engaging in cognitive control is experienced as effortful and induces fatigue. Here, we tested the hypothesis that sustained activation in the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (DLPFC)—a neural substrate of cognitive control—causally induces motivational fatigue via the accumulation of prefrontal glutamate metabolites. For this purpose, we combined brain stimulation with spectroscopy imaging to assess how increasing DLPFC excitability during an effortful mental task changes the motivation for mental effort and glutamate concentrations. We found that stimulating the DLPFC during mental effort exertion improved mental performance at the cost of increased posteffort motivational fatigue, suggesting a causal role of DLPFC activation for inducing fatigue. On the neural level, DLPFC activation during effortful cognition also increased prefrontal concentrations of glutamate, which statistically explained the fatigue-induced lower motivation for mental effort. A corresponding analysis of combined glutamate–glutamine (Glx) concentrations revealed converging effects. Together, these findings provide causal evidence that enhanced DLPFC activation contributes to fatigue via neurochemical changes, supporting neuro-metabolic accounts of fatigue and offering new insights into why demanding cognitive tasks are perceived as effortful.

articles_hidden.title: Hepatocyte-derived exosomal miR-122 mediates liver-to-brain crosstalk and neuroinflammation in alcohol-exposed Alzheimer’s disease mice
articles_hidden.authors: Veronika Brezani, Marti Ortega-Ribera, Neda Rezagholizadeh, Radhika Joshi, Viliam Brezani, Mrigya Babuta, Bruna de Araujo Cardoso dos Santos, Adam Zivny, Prashanth Thevkar Nagesh, Ionita Ghiran, Elizabeth Michelle Shreyer, Scott Brian Minchenberg, Allyson Flavin, Gyongyi Szabo
articles_hidden.abstract: Neuroinflammation and microglial activation are common features in Alzheimer’s disease (AD) and excessive alcohol consumption. Alcohol induces liver damage and inflammation, and altered serum aminotransferases have been reported in patients with AD. Small extracellular vesicles (sEVs) and their cargo are emerging as mediators of intercellular communication in AD and alcohol-induced liver injury. However, the effects of alcohol use on AD progression remain to be elucidated. In this study, we evaluated the effects of repeated binge drinking on the liver and brain in the APP/PS1 mouse model of AD. Alcohol-exposed APP/PS1 mice showed elevated serum alanine aminotransferase levels, indicating liver injury absent in controls, along with increased pro-inflammatory cytokine expression in both liver and brain. Alcohol increased the biogenesis and release of sEVs in AD mice and in mouse hepatocytes. These sEVs were enriched in mature miR-122-5p that is predominant in hepatocytes. In vivo, miR-122-5p was detected in the brain of alcohol-exposed AD mice suggesting EV-mediated miR-122-5p transfer to the brain. Microglial uptake of hepatocyte-derived sEVs was confirmed in vitro. sEVs from alcohol-treated hepatocytes sensitized BV-2 microglia to LPS stimulation, significantly enhancing CCL2, CXCL2, CCL3, and TNF-α production. Transfection of microglia with a miR-122-5p mimic partially recapitulated the pro-inflammatory sensitization by sEVs from alcohol-exposed hepatocytes, which was reversed by miR-122-5p inhibitor delivery. ADAM10, a miR-122-5p target, was reduced in both wild-type and AD brains after alcohol exposure, with cell-specific effects. These results suggest that alcohol-induced hepatocyte-derived sEVs may modulate liver-to-brain signaling via miR-122-5p and contribute to neuroinflammation in AD.

articles_hidden.title: Binding sites as dynamic hubs of coevolution encoded information flow
articles_hidden.authors: Kemal Demirtaş, Burak Erman, Türkan Haliloğlu
articles_hidden.abstract: The relationship between evolution and allostery is inherently intertwined. While structural studies have elucidated allosteric mechanisms, the extent to which evolutionary sequence information encodes these dynamic networks remains underexplored. Here, we introduce Sequence-based GNM-TE, a framework that integrates coevolutionary information with Gaussian Network Model (GNM) based Transfer Entropy (TE) calculations. This approach translates evolutionary constraints, shaped by both structural and functional requirements, into functionally meaningful allosteric dynamic information. Across 29 cases, we identify binding sites as dynamic hubs of collective information transfer and reveal mode-dependent, directional information flows between these sites. These findings overall indicate that evolutionary constraints embed the architecture of allosteric regulation within protein sequences, preserving binding site communication within layered dynamic ensembles that enable robust functional control and adaptation.

articles_hidden.title: On-site, subannual climate records decouple Neolithic expansion from climate instability
articles_hidden.authors: Niklas Hausmann, Danai Theodoraki
articles_hidden.abstract: How the life of prehistoric people was influenced by climate change and extreme events often remains elusive. Finding appropriate spatiotemporal scales is the major challenge for studies with socioenvironmental questions. This challenge can be overcome by sourcing climatic information from archaeological sites, alongside traces of human agency. For instance, extreme cold-events have been proposed as causing a standstill in early farming expansion across the Mediterranean 8600-8000 years ago. However, there is no immediate (local/short-term) evidence of such events and how they might have influenced people’s lives, nor have previous records been sufficiently resolved to test this robustly. Here we statistically assess the influence of on-site and short-term extremes on human decision-making hypothesized by long-term climate records. Using the largest dataset yet of high-resolution temperature archives in mollusks, we test whether early farmers would have been exposed to extreme cold-events, compromising their subsistence by reducing harvest yields. This immediate agricultural risk is argued to have prevented the spread of new settlements and thus delayed the vigorous expansion that followed, one of prehistory’s fastest known dispersals. Direct comparison of paleotemperature and subsistence data from the same archaeological contexts shows no winter cooling of the magnitude proposed for this period, and no strong relationship between climate and subsistence. Our study reveals how a major scale mismatch in climate-society research can be resolved at the site level, integrating climatic variability on the subannual timescale crucial to farming, and provides a direct, local empirical test of a long-assumed climate impact.

articles_hidden.title: Kinome profiling enabled development of a LATS1/2 inhibitor with wound healing potential
articles_hidden.authors: Frances A. Tosto, Patrick J. Morris, Yanyan Qu, Lale Evsen, Gregory J. Tawa, Ravi Tharakan, Bridget S. Scherer, Damien Y. Duveau, Dvir Blivis, Ty Voss, Ganesha Rai, Mahfuza Sharmin, Dingyin Tao, Christopher A. LeClair, Leonid Peshkin, Taranjit S. Gujral, Ana Corrionero, Scott B. Hoyt, Marc W. Kirschner, Craig J. Thomas, Michele Ceribelli
articles_hidden.abstract: System-level mapping of kinase inhibitors’ polypharmacology can uncover opportunities for drug repurposing and identify starting points for medicinal chemistry campaigns aimed at novel targets. Here, we describe a large-scale profiling of 257 kinase inhibitors that revealed domains of promiscuity, a broad region of uninhibited targets and discrete pockets of selectivity. Focusing on a subcluster enriched for AGC group kinases and using the AKT inhibitor AT-7867 (an antiproliferative agent) as a starting point, we employed scaffold hopping and property-based optimization to discover NCGC-6782, a LATS1/2 inhibitor with robust proproliferative activity. In biochemical and cell-based assays, NCGC-6782 inhibited LATS1/2 activity, reduced YAP phosphorylation, and promoted rapid YAP nuclear translocation and transactivation of YAP-target genes. Kinome-wide profilings demonstrated good in vitro selectivity and exquisite chemoproteomic and kinetic selectivity. In vivo, NCGC-6782 exhibited favorable pharmacokinetic (PK) profiles following intraperitoneal (IP), intravenous (IV), or oral (PO) dosing, leading to rapid inhibition of YAP-phosphorylation in murine liver samples. Transcriptomics and proteomics following NCGC-6782 revealed upregulation of YAP-dependent genes (4 h) followed by activation of cell cycle programs (24 h). Consistently, NCGC-6782 accelerated proliferative regeneration in both cell-based and in vivo wound healing models of full-thickness excisional skin injury, significantly shortening wound-closure time without evidence of systemic toxicity. Altogether, we describe an optimized, potent, and selective LATS1/2 kinase inhibitor with desirable drug-like properties and broad potential for regenerative medicine applications following acute injury of nonproliferative, postmitotic tissues.

articles_hidden.title: The purinergic receptor P2Y 13 controls the activation and mode of division of adult ventricular–subventricular zone neural stem cells
articles_hidden.authors: Lucía Paniagua-Herranz, Julia Serrano-López, Celia Llorente-Sáez, Marina Leonor Pérez-Sanz, David de Agustín-Durán, Pere Duart-Abadia, Ana Domingo-Muelas, África Vincelle-Nieto, Paloma Bragado, Diana Manzano-Franco, Marina Arribas-Blázquez, Lucía Gallego, Araceli Garcia-Mora, Luis Alcides Olivos-Oré, Sergio Gascón, Álvaro Gutierrez-Uzquiza, Benedikt Berninger, Raquel Pérez-Sen, Esmerilda G. Delicado, Rosa Gómez-Villafuertes, Armando Reyes-Palomares, Antonio R. Artalejo, Isabel Fariñas, Felipe Ortega
articles_hidden.abstract: The ventricular–subventricular zone (V-SVZ) is the most active germinal area in the mammalian brain and it continues to generate newborn neurons throughout life. This area harbors a population of neural stem cells (NSCs) that exist in different states of activation: quiescent NSCs, primed NSCs, and activated NSCs. There are currently few specific markers to effectively discern each state. Likewise, the molecular signals that control the transition from quiescence to activation remain largely unexplored, and the factors that controls whether dividing NSCs differentiate or self-renew are poorly understood. Here, we present evidence that the metabotropic P2Y 13 purinergic receptor plays a critical role in regulating adult neurogenesis. We found that P2Y 13 is specifically expressed in NSCs within the adult V-SVZ and that its levels can be used to distinguish quiescent from activated NSCs. P2Y 13 signaling promotes NSC activation, enhancing lineage progression as opposed to their self-renewal. Conversely, pharmacological blockade or genetic silencing of P2Y 13 receptors favors NSC quiescence. Thus, we consider the metabotropic P2Y 13 purinergic receptor a pivotal modulator of NSC dynamics.

articles_hidden.title: In-context learning as a retraining-free paradigm for constitutive modeling
articles_hidden.authors: Lingfeng Li, Zhuoyuan Li, Shun Li, Kaixin Zhan, Huajian Gao, Chang Qing Chen, Liu Yang
articles_hidden.abstract: Constitutive modeling is fundamental to computational solid mechanics, yet most existing approaches remain material-specific and require retraining or recalibration when materials change. Here we introduce In-Context Modeling (ICM), a retraining-free paradigm for constitutive modeling that infers constitutive behavior from physical context rather than material-specific optimization. Using hyperelasticity as a testbed, we demonstrate that ICM can be trained once on equilibrium deformation fields spanning diverse materials, geometries, and boundary conditions, enforcing physical equilibrium without stress labels. After training, the same model can be directly deployed on previously unseen hyperelastic materials without retraining. At inference, ICM treats a small set of nonuniform strain fields as physical context to generate constitutive response in a single forward pass. Numerical benchmarks and experimental validation demonstrate accurate stress prediction across out-of-distribution materials and boundary-value problems, together with substantial reductions in deployment cost compared with per-material learning approaches. These results establish in-context learning as a retraining-free paradigm for constitutive modeling, particularly valuable for heterogeneous biological tissues such as the brain, and suggest a pathway toward foundation models for computational mechanics.

articles_hidden.title: Mark A. Ratner (1942–2026): Founded molecular electronics while spearheading the growth of science at Northwestern University
articles_hidden.authors: Gemma C. Solomon, George C. Schatz
articles_hidden.abstract: Recently, we lost one of the original developers of the field of molecular electronics. Mark A. Ratner wrote a famous paper in 1974 that developed the theoretical framework for making a molecule act as a rectifier. This idea, and a host of further ideas that were stimulated by this and other papers, led to a huge amount of experimental and theoretical studies that continue to this day. But Mark’s career was much more than that, with leadership at Northwestern University and beyond that continues to shape the scientific enterprise.

articles_hidden.title: Reply to Cirillo: Early-life exposure to the sugar-rationing regime, not a measured sugar dose, drives the cancer gradient
articles_hidden.authors: Chen Zhu, Weilong Zhang

articles_hidden.title: An aggregation-prone region in talin controls talin self-interactions and regulates integrin adhesion complex dynamics
articles_hidden.authors: Neil J. Ball, Paula Turkki, Yanyu Guo, Mahmudul H. Tanvir, Shimin Le, Jasmine Fei Li Chin, Karen B. Baker, Jingxing Luo, Paul Atherton, Nicholas H. Brown, Vesa P. Hytönen, Jie Yan, Benjamin T. Goult
articles_hidden.abstract: Talin is a mechanosensitive scaffold that couples integrins to the actin cytoskeleton and coordinates signaling at integrin adhesion complexes. A second integrin-binding site (IBS2) has been proposed within the R11–R12 region of the talin rod, although the molecular basis of this interaction has remained unclear. Here, we show that talin R11 contains a cryptic aggregation-prone region (APR) embedded within Helix50. Mechanical unfolding of R11 exposes this motif, enabling high-affinity talin–talin interactions and force-dependent self-association. The isolated APR forms amyloid-like fibers in vitro, and APR-disrupting gatekeeper mutations suppress fiber formation, talin self-association, and cellular recruitment. We therefore designate this motif Aggregation-Prone Region 1 (APR1). Mitochondrial-targeting experiments demonstrate that APR1-dependent recruitment occurs in cells independently of focal adhesions and integrins. APR1 overlaps the vinculin-binding site in Helix50, and vinculin disrupts preexisting talin assemblies, revealing a mechano-chaperone function for vinculin. Disruption of APR1-mediated self-association does not impair adhesion formation but instead generates larger, more talin-rich adhesions with altered assembly dynamics and signaling properties, indicating a role for APR1 in regulating adhesion remodeling. Together, these findings identify force-dependent talin self-association as a mechanism in mechanotransduction and suggest that the region previously designated IBS2 functions primarily as an aggregation-prone regulatory element.

articles_hidden.title: Entropic tightening of knots in granular chains under vibration
articles_hidden.authors: Qiyuan Qiu, Yujie Zheng, Jiansong Yang, Peng Hua, Yilong Han, Liang Dai
articles_hidden.abstract: Knots are common in long chains, from DNA and proteins to everyday strings, yet direct observation of knot dynamics is difficult. Using granular chains on vibrating platforms, we directly visualize knot dynamics and find that knot cores spontaneously tighten, a behavior observed across different knot types. We quantitatively explain spontaneous knot tightening using knot-tube theory: segments confined within the knot core experience entropic loss and tend to escape the core to gain conformational entropy. Although driven granular chains are not in thermodynamic equilibrium, their steady-state knot-size statistics are approximately captured by equilibrium statistical mechanics and Monte Carlo simulations. Analyses of state-transition probabilities and time-reversal asymmetry suggest a weak violation of detailed balance when the granular dynamics are projected onto the knot-size coordinate. Finally, we discuss the possible relevance of knot tightening to topoisomerase-mediated DNA unknotting.

articles_hidden.title: Dynamic virulence decomposition disentangles host and pathogen contributions over the course of infection
articles_hidden.authors: Mathias Franz, Camille Bonneaud
articles_hidden.abstract: Decomposing virulence into host and pathogen effects is key to understanding how virulence is generated during infection, and how host and pathogen contributions evolve over time. Conventional virulence decomposition is, however, not designed to quantify how these contributions vary throughout an infection. Building on conventional virulence decomposition, we developed a dynamic framework that integrates disease space analysis to quantify these changing contributions. We applied this framework to existing data from house finches ( Haemorhous mexicanus ) experimentally infected with the emerging bacterial pathogen, Mycoplasma gallisepticum , examining two biologically meaningful infection phases: an early phase dominated by innate immune responses and a later phase in which the adaptive immune response is fully activated. Our analyses revealed that virulence components evolved differently across infection phases, with pathogen exploitation, per-parasite-pathogenicity (PPP), and host resistance each exhibiting distinct trajectories. These findings corroborated several known evolutionary patterns, while also revealing the evolution of increased PPP in this system. In contrast, the apparent evolution of host tolerance inferred from aggregated peak measurements was not supported by phase-specific analyses, demonstrating that aggregated and phase-specific measures can provide different mechanistic insights into virulence. By linking conventional virulence decomposition with disease space analysis, our dynamic virulence decomposition framework provides a general approach for quantifying how host and pathogen processes shape virulence over the course of infection.

articles_hidden.title: Structural basis of glycoprotein recognition by the human folding sensor UDP-glucose:glycoprotein glucosyltransferase
articles_hidden.authors: David Aparicio, Juan R. Ortigosa, Kevin P. Guay, Robert V. Williams, Jorge O. Lannot, Guanghui Zong, Natalia Comino, José F. Rodríguez, Lai-Xi Wang, Marcelo A. Martí, Pietro Roversi, Daniel N. Hebert, Lila M. Gierasch, Carlos P. Modenutti, Marcelo E. Guerin
articles_hidden.abstract: UDP-glucose:glycoprotein glucosyltransferase 1 (UGGT1) plays a central role in quality control of glycoprotein folding within the early secretory pathway, yet the molecular basis of UGGT1 substrate recognition remains poorly understood. Here, we report cryo-EM structures of human full-length multidomain UGGT1. Monomeric UGGT1 structures reveal two conformational states corresponding to “open” and “closed” architectures. Three-dimensional variability and molecular dynamics simulations suggest the existence of intermediate conformations, leading to a model in which a continuum of structural transitions underlies UGGT1 function. Notably, in the open state, the EM-maps reveal at the top of the U-shaped protein a density that bridges the sensory TRXL2 and the glucosyltransferase catalytic domains, consistent with substrate association. This observation supports a mode of binding that places the substrate near the catalytic domain. A dimeric form of UGGT1 was observed in which the glycoprotein substrate binding sites are occluded, suggesting that dimerization may regulate UGGT1 activity. To better understand the spatial relationship between the site of misfolding and that of UGGT-mediated N-glycan reglucosylation, we identified N-glycosylation sites on endogenous glycoprotein substrates by glycoproteomics. No consensus sequence was found flanking modified sites, indicating that substrate recognition relies on mechanisms beyond primary sequence. Mutations in the UGGT1 gene cause a novel congenital disorder of glycosylation characterized by developmental delay and intellectual disability, and the human UGGT1 structure helps explain how disease-associated missense and deletion variants disrupt function. Together, our data provide insight into the relationship between UGGT1 structure and function, integrating enzyme conformational states with client glycoprotein interaction and processing.

articles_hidden.title: Intratumoral cDC1–T cell clusters serve as sites of local costimulation to enhance CTL-mediated tumor rejection
articles_hidden.authors: Catherine B. Carbone, Markus Brown, Camille-Charlotte Balança, Anthony C. Antonelli, Shiuh-Ming Luoh, Karl L. Banta, Vincent Rouilly, Ximo Pechuan-Jorge, Guadalupe Ortiz-Muñoz, Jeanne Cheung, Ines Marin, Ellen Duong, Aditya A. Anand, Rajiv Jesudason, Caleb K. Chan, Anugraha Rajagopalan, Justin T. Gibson, Amanda Lorentzian, Elisa Penna, Jian Jiang, Linda Rangell, Yuxin Liang, Jérémie Decalf, Rosa Barreira da Silva, Ying Zhu, Shannon J. Turley, Geraldine A. Strasser, Sandra Rost, Shomyseh Sanjabi, James Ziai, Kathryn Geiger-Schuller, Lélia Delamarre, Ira Mellman, Christine Moussion
articles_hidden.abstract: T cells are essential for antitumor immunity, but their ability to eliminate tumors depends on interactions with type 1 conventional dendritic cells (cDC1s). cDC1s are known for cross-presenting tumor-derived antigens in lymph nodes to prime T cells, but their role within tumors remains less well understood. Here, we use a tumor array model to investigate how cDC1–T cell interactions influence immune responses and tumor fate. We show that the spatial distribution of both cDC1s and T cells determines whether a tumor can be rejected. We defined three immunotypes based on the spatial distribution of T cells and cDC1s: T cell–inflamed/dendritic cell-inflamed (TC-In/DC-In) tumors, where T cells and cDC1s coinfiltrate the tumor; T cell–inflamed/dendritic cell-excluded (TC-In/DC-Ex) tumors, where T cells infiltrate but cDC1s remain at the periphery; and T cell–excluded/dendritic cell-excluded (TC-Ex/DC-Ex) tumors, which lack both cDC1 and T cell infiltration. TC-In/DC-In tumors are most likely to undergo rejection, whereas TC-In/DC-Ex tumors persist despite T cell infiltration. Within TC-In/DC-In tumors, cDC1s interact directly with T cells, upregulate costimulatory molecules, and sustain effector T cell responses, while cDC1s in TC-In/DC-Ex tumors express higher migration-associated genes, suggesting they may exit the tumor. We further show that chemokine modulation, particularly through CXCL9, CCL5, and XCL1, can reshape immune infiltration patterns to promote intratumoral cDC1–T cell clustering and improve tumor rejection. These findings reveal an important role of cDC1 in sustaining effective antitumor immunity and highlight spatially organized cDC1–T cell clusters as critical hubs for local T cell activation.

articles_hidden.title: Maize genetic diversity is largely unstructured by human ethnolinguistic diversity in its center of origin
articles_hidden.authors: Samantha J. Snodgrass, Forrest Li, Sowmya Mambakkam, Santiago G. Medina-Muñoz, Luke Sparreo, Mitra Menon, Claudia Perez, Namrata Kalsi, Amit G. Ghosh, Stephan C. Schuster, Hie Lim Kim, Andrés Moreno-Estrada, Daniel E. Runcie, Graham Coop, Jeffrey Ross-Ibarra
articles_hidden.abstract: Population structure and environmental features often capture major axes of genetic variation in many species. Yet the impacts of human activity often remain unquantified. For domesticated species that rely on human activity for survival and dispersal, human movements and cultural differences may play key roles patterning genetic diversity. Maize is a staple crop of enormous cultural importance to indigenous peoples of the Americas, but cannot survive or disperse without farmers. Using publicly available genotyping and passport data from approximately 2,000 traditional maize varieties, more than 500 whole genome sequences of humans from Mexico, and indigenous linguistic maps, we quantify anthropogenic effects on maize genetic diversity in the Americas. Maize shows very little overall structure, highlighting the effectiveness of indigenous farmers in moving and mixing maize populations. While principal components of maize diversity show meaningful correlations to human genetic diversity, our linear modeling suggests little additional impact of human population structure beyond shared geography. Though differences in maize diversity are often patterned by language locally, we find only weak genome-wide effects at larger spatial scales. Despite the relatively weak global signal of anthropogenic effects, linguistic Genome-wide association, outlier F ST analyses, and selection scans identified loci associated with specific languages. Leveraging landscape-level sequencing data, we highlight how anthropogenic factors have shaped patterns of maize genetic diversity across Mesoamerica.

articles_hidden.title: A DPY19L2/FAM209-associated protein–Arp complex–CAPZA3 scaffold is essential for perinuclear theca assembly and fertilization
articles_hidden.authors: Tiechao Ruan, Gan Shen, Liangchai Zhuo, Yingteng Zhang, Xiang Wang, Erpo Tian, Yunchuan Tian, Xinyao Tang, Daijuan Chen, Chuan Jiang, Xue Yang, Jun Ma, Shikun Zhao, Chanjuan Zhao, Xinyue Cui, Xiaohui Jiang, Yihong Yang, Yan Wang, Ying Shen
articles_hidden.abstract: Fertilization is a fundamental biological process that enables the fusion of a spermatozoon with an oocyte to initiate embryonic development. However, the underlying mechanisms leading to fertilization failure remain poorly understood. Here, we demonstrated that the actin-related protein (Arp) family members ACTRT2 and ACTRT3 are essential for fertilization in both humans and mice, whereas ACTL10 is dispensable for fertility and the human-specific ACTL8 may play a role in early spermatogenesis. Ultrastructural and immunofluorescence analyses revealed that, during spermatogenesis, ACTRT2 or ACTRT3 deficiency disrupts the assembly of subacrosomal layer of the perinuclear theca (SAL-PT), leading to acrosome detachment and subsequent manchette abnormalities, which in turn impairs the formation of the postacrosomal sheath of the PT. These structural defects were accompanied by reduced abundance of the candidate sperm-borne oocyte-activating factors PAWP and PLCζ. Moreover, knockout of Actrt2 or Actrt3 severely impaired spermatozoa’s ability to penetrate the zona pellucida during in vitro fertilization. Mechanistically, ACTRT2, ACTRT3, ACTL7A, ACTL7B, and ACTL9 form a testis-enriched Arp complex in the SAL-PT and maintain the stability of one another. This complex interacts with the PT protein CAPZA3, which subsequently binds and stabilizes PLCζ. Additionally, the Arp complex interacts with DPY19L2/FAM209-associated proteins to mediate acrosome anchoring to the nuclear envelope. Therefore, these findings established a sequential DPY19L2/FAM209-associated protein–Arp complex–CAPZA3 scaffold extending from the nuclear envelope to the acrosome that is indispensable for fertilization. Collectively, we defined a previously unidentified structural and molecular framework for fertilization and provided insights into the diagnosis and treatment of fertilization failure.

articles_hidden.title: Amphipathic helices repurpose a Patched/NPC1-like cholesterol transporter to function at Plasmodium –erythrocyte membrane contact sites
articles_hidden.authors: Ananya Ray, Eva S. Istvan, Daniel E. Goldberg, Matthias Garten
articles_hidden.abstract: The interface between the malaria parasite Plasmodium spp. and its host erythrocyte critically mediates nutrient uptake, lipid exchange, and protein export required for parasite replication and thus pathogenesis. Approximately half of this interface consists of narrow membrane contact sites, a region defined by only 3 to 4 nm of aqueous space between the parasite plasma membrane and the parasitophorous vacuole membrane. Despite its extent, the region remains largely uncharacterized and inaccessible, not least due to its narrowness. The sole identified resident is the Plasmodium falciparum Niemann-Pick Type C1-Related protein, PfNCR1, an essential Patched/NPC1-like cholesterol transporter, suggesting this conserved transporter family has evolved an unconventional adaptation for localizing to membrane contact sites that can reveal a mechanism to access the region. Here, using live-cell microscopy and assessment of cholesterol homeostasis, we identify a helix–linker–helix (HLH) domain as the necessary modification for efficient PfNCR1 localization. We find that correct localization is required for the parasite to maintain low cholesterol levels, connecting targeting to function. Using a glycosylphosphatidylinositol-anchored fluorescent reporter as a minimal membrane-associated protein, we show that the HLH domain is sufficient to drive localization to the narrow membrane contact site region. Mechanistically, we demonstrate that targeting depends on the physicochemical character of the targeting domain rather than a specific primary sequence, identifying amphipathicity as a determining property of the HLH domain. Taken together, we propose physicochemical partitioning as a fundamental principle for protein targeting at the Plasmodium –erythrocyte interface, and for driving direct functional interactions of a Patched/NPC1-like protein with a second membrane.

articles_hidden.title: Dissociation of gravity and limb dynamics in motor control
articles_hidden.authors: Valeriya Gritsenko, Tjaša Kunavar, Marko Jamšek, Sergiy Yakovenko, Olivier White, Jan Babič
articles_hidden.abstract: Human movements remain accurate across substantial variations in mechanical loading, yet how the nervous system anticipates and compensates for intrinsic and extrinsic forces when generating muscle commands remains unresolved. Because the forces acting on the body are complex and nonlinear, dynamical modeling provides a powerful framework for identifying the computations underlying motor control. Here, we exploited parabolic flight to dissociate gravitational loading from intrinsic limb dynamics and directly test how these mechanical components are represented in motor commands. We analyzed kinematics and shoulder muscle activity from nine participants performing visually guided pointing movements in microgravity (0g), normogravity (1g), and hypergravity (2g). Inverse dynamics revealed that the gravity-independent component of muscle torque remained invariant across gravitational conditions. In striking contrast, muscle moments estimated from muscle activation showed systematic scaling of not only static but also phasic components with gravitational load, particularly during movement deceleration. This divergence arises because activation-derived muscle moments capture cocontraction, and thus impedance-related control, that is absent from net torques obtained by inverse dynamics. Gravity-dependent regression analyses further showed that muscle activation could be reconstructed from a compact set of mechanical variables dominated by gravity-dependent torque and movement velocity, revealing a low-dimensional structure of motor control. Together, these findings support a control architecture in which motor commands integrate predictive compensation for limb dynamics with gravity-dependent regulation of muscle cocontraction. This dual strategy provides a mechanism for maintaining stable and accurate movement across changing mechanical environments and offers a unified framework for understanding motor control under variable external loads.

articles_hidden.title: Afforestation reshapes wildfire activity across global temperate biomes
articles_hidden.authors: Irene Repeto-Deudero, Alejandro Miranda, Juli G. Pausas, Carlos Hormazábal, Blas Mola-Yudego, Javier Lopatin, Susana Gómez-González
articles_hidden.abstract: In temperate ecosystems, afforestation is rapidly expanding as a flagship climate mitigation strategy. Yet its impact on wildfires remains poorly understood, raising concerns that establishing planted forests over nonforest areas may intensify wildfire activity under increasingly fire-prone climatic conditions. Here, we combine land-use change data, fire activity records, climatic and anthropogenic covariates to quantify how afforestation alters fire occurrence and burned area across 67,248 patches distributed throughout global temperate biomes using satellite records starting in 2001. We found that, on average, afforestation increased fire occurrence by 26% and burned area by 23% in global temperate regions. However, these effects differed markedly among biomes. Wildfire responses ranged from a near-threefold increase in fire occurrence in Temperate Conifer Forests and a 38% increase in Mediterranean Woodlands biomes to an 18% reduction in the Temperate Grasslands, Savannas, and Shrublands biome. In Temperate Broadleaf and Mixed Forests, afforestation reduced fire occurrence but increased burned area, indicating a shift toward less frequent but larger wildfires following the conversion to planted forest. These contrasting, biome-specific responses show that the consequences of afforestation on wildfire activity may depend strongly on ecological and regional context. The strong variability at biome-scale questions the premise that tree planting provides consistent climate mitigation benefits across all landscapes, and highlights the need to evaluate afforestation initiatives alongside regional disturbance regimes. Our findings indicate that wildfire risk should be explicitly accounted for when assessing the long-term effectiveness of afforestation as a climate mitigation strategy in a warming world.

articles_hidden.title: Pericyte contraction generates angiostatic effect via cell force–dependent activation of TGFβ
articles_hidden.authors: Carole Y. Perrot, Shahidul Islam, Joanne E. Murphy-Ullrich, Masanobu Komatsu
articles_hidden.abstract: Pericytes are phenotypically plastic and capable of switching between contractile and proliferative phenotypes, similar to vascular smooth muscle cells. The intimate interaction of contractile pericytes with endothelial cells (ECs) is essential to the maturation, quiescence, and stability of the capillary and microvascular endothelium. However, the mechanistic link between pericyte contraction and vascular stability is unknown. It is known that TGFβ has dual pro- and antiangiogenic effects depending on the downstream Smad signaling. Here, we show that R-Ras-mediated contractility in pericytes activates TGFβ by integrin-dependent, actomyosin-generated cell traction force. This TGFβ activation, in turn, promotes the quiescence of ECs via the ALK5-Smad2/3 axis of the TGFβ pathway in ECs, but not the Smad1/5 axis of the TGFβ pathway. Furthermore, pericyte-targeted deletion of Rras in mice resulted in impaired pericyte contractility and a significant reduction of Smad2/3 phosphorylation in ECs, accompanied by increased tumor angiogenesis and vessel deformation in the skeletal muscle. These observations suggest that pericytes use the cell force to maintain the quiescence of the endothelium by elevating the local bioavailability of active TGFβ. Our findings provide a mechanism by which pericytes stabilize blood vessels.

articles_hidden.title: The limits of scaling in aggregation-driven patterning of cell collectives
articles_hidden.authors: Michael L. Zhao, Jan Rombouts, Anniek Stokkermans, Anna Erzberger, Alexander Aulehla
articles_hidden.abstract: Robust development requires maintaining correct proportions as overall size varies. What controls and limits this scaling remains poorly understood due to the complex interplay of mechanical and biochemical embryonic factors. Combining confinement of dissociated embryonic presomitic mesoderm cells with imaging and chemical perturbations, we identified cell aggregation as the initial event in de novo posterior pole formation. Using a continuum model based solely on cell–cell attraction, we quantitatively map how the time available for aggregation-driven patterning limits the maximum scalable system size. Small systems allow rapid, robust pattern scaling, whereas coarsening dynamics substantially delay scaled patterns in large systems. Our experiments quantitatively confirm these predicted scaling regimes. Together, our results reveal a developmental time–size tradeoff governing the scaling of aggregation-driven patterns.

articles_hidden.title: TLR7-independent control of retroviral infection
articles_hidden.authors: Robert Z. Zhang, Lia Robben, Ashley Willey, Sandra Umana, Vincent Mele, Brady Callahan, Tatyana Golovkina, Kevin R. McCarthy, Melissa Kane
articles_hidden.abstract: Development of effective immune responses against any pathogen requires efficient activation of the innate immune system followed by induction of an appropriate adaptive immune response using specific signaling pathways tailored to each infection. The sole innate immune receptor implicated in the induction of adaptive immunity to retroviral infection is Toll-like receptor 7 (TLR7). We have found that germinal center responses, neutralizing antibody production, and clearance of murine leukemia virus (MLV) infection in BALB.J and C57BL/6N (B6N) mice occurs in the absence of TLR7 signaling. This suggests that a previously unknown alternative sensing pathway exists for the activation of protective immune responses upon retroviral infection. Genetic crosses indicate that the ability to control retroviral infection in the absence of TLR7 signaling is determined by the same recessive mechanism in both B6N and BALB.J mice, suggesting that TLR7-independent responses do not result from a gain-of-function of an alternative pattern recognition receptor. Additionally, we observed that TLR7-deficient BALB.J mice produce neutralizing antibodies against mouse mammary tumor virus (MMTV) infection, indicating that this alternative sensing pathway is active against retroviruses of multiple genera. Finally, we determined that the alternative sensing pathway is also independent of both MyD88 and STING signaling. The ability of mice of two genetic backgrounds to control retroviral infection in the absence of TLR7 signaling provides a valuable tool for the identification of an additional mechanism of retrovirus control. The dissection of this pathway has the potential to alter our understanding of the requirements for the stimulation of antigen-specific neutralizing immunity.

articles_hidden.title: Municipal sludge disposal emerges as a major, hidden, and rapidly growing atmospheric mercury source
articles_hidden.authors: Xingrui Cai, Mengqi Yang, Maodian Liu, Shijun Ma, Xinran Qiu, Qianru Zhang, Xuejun Wang
articles_hidden.abstract: Wastewater treatment greatly reduces mercury pollution in aquatic ecosystems but does not eliminate it. Here, we identify municipal sludge disposal as a major, long-overlooked atmospheric mercury source. In China, sludge disposal emitted 42 - 10 + 18 Mg in 2024, exceeding 10% of national anthropogenic emissions and ranking third after cement production and nonferrous metal smelting. These emissions have increased by nearly a thousandfold since the 1970s and are concentrated in densely populated urban areas, driven by the rapid expansion of sludge incineration, codisposal, and composting. Our findings reveal a cross-media pollution transfer embedded in sustainability transitions and call for sludge disposal to be incorporated into UNEP mercury budget and Minamata Convention assessments.

articles_hidden.title: Polarized twin walls in a halide perovskite
articles_hidden.authors: Weilun Li, Qimu Yuan, Michael B. Johnston, Joanne Etheridge
articles_hidden.abstract: Halide perovskites have emerged as promising materials for next-generation photovoltaics, laser sources, and X-ray detectors. There is intense debate as to whether some photoactive halide perovskites exhibit ferroelectric behavior and whether it might be possible to utilize the bulk photovoltaic effect to enhance the performance of halide perovskite solar cells. Here, using low-dose scanning transmission electron microscopy, we identify ferroelastic twin walls in vapor-deposited CsPbI 3 thin films, parallel to {110} and {112}. Remarkably, despite CsPbI 3 being centrosymmetric and nonpolar, we observe directly that Pb atoms shift at {110} twin walls driving a local ferroelectric-like polarization. These polar twin walls form an intrinsic array of nanoscale interfaces, spaced ~30 to 50 nm apart, embedded within the nonpolar perovskite lattice. In contrast, {112} twin walls do not show a polar displacement of Pb but strongly suppress octahedral tilt and off-center Cs atom displacements, revealing a different untapped structural degree of freedom. These findings reveal previously hidden nanoscale polarization in halide perovskite semiconductors, opening opportunities for enhanced conductivity and photovoltaic behavior through domain wall engineering.

articles_hidden.title: Thermodynamic stabilization of substrate protein within the GroEL:ES chaperonin cage
articles_hidden.authors: Wei Xue, Andreas Bracher, F. Ulrich Hartl, Manajit Hayer-Hartl
articles_hidden.abstract: The adenosine triphosphate (ATP)-regulated GroEL/ES chaperonin of Escherichia coli promotes protein folding by transiently encapsulating unfolded substrate protein in a nano-cage formed by the cylindrical GroEL and the lid-shaped GroES. How this confinement modulates the folding energy landscape, allowing accelerated protein folding unimpaired by aggregation, remains incompletely understood. Prompted by recent observations suggesting that the chaperonin cavity may favor unfolding [I. Korobko et al. , Proc. Natl. Acad. Sci. U.S.A. 119 , e2213170119 (2022)], here we reinvestigated the effect of encapsulation on protein thermodynamic stability. To allow thermal unfolding of an encapsulated substrate protein, we generated a destabilized variant of maltose-binding protein (MBP) by introducing four mutations, quadruple mutant-MBP (QM-MBP), lowering the melting temperature ( T m ) from 63.6 °C to 44.3 °C. GroEL/ES accelerated the slow spontaneous folding of QM-MBP ~20-fold. The protein reached a native-like structure while encapsulated inside GroEL:ES, as demonstrated using hydrogen/deuterium exchange and single molecule fluorescence resonance energy transfer analyses in presence and absence of the ligand maltose. Importantly, confinement in the thermally stable chaperonin shifted the cooperative unfolding transition of QM-MBP to a T m of 52.4 °C, corresponding to a stabilization by 4.6 kcal mol −1 . In-cage thermal unfolding was reversible, indicating that the environment of the chaperonin cavity is conducive to folding. These findings suggest that a thermodynamically stabilizing effect of the GroEL:ES cage contributes to promoting protein folding.

articles_hidden.title: CD8 + regulatory T cells limit immunopathology but impair viral clearance in Hantaan virus infection
articles_hidden.authors: Kang Tang, Xiaoyue Xu, He Liu, Yun Zhang, Yusi Zhang, Chunmei Zhang, Kai Li, Jiajia Zuo, Kexuan Zhao, Xuyang Zheng, Fenglan Wang, Ran Zhuang, Lihua Chen, Fanglin Zhang, Ying Ma
articles_hidden.abstract: In hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) caused by Hantaan virus (HTNV), virus-specific CD8 + T cells mediate both viral clearance and immunopathology. Here, we characterized a CD8 + regulatory T cell (Treg) subset restricted by HLA-E (and its murine ortholog Qa-1) in HFRS patients and in a murine HTNV infection model. CD8 + Tregs (CD122 + Eomes + CD49d lo KIR + ), a subset substantially enriched for HLA-E-restricted T cells, were significantly reduced in peripheral blood of HFRS patients and displayed a terminally differentiated profile with elevated expression of KLRG-1, NKG2A, CTLA-4, and Fas-L, correlating with disease severity. Two HTNV glycoprotein-derived nonapeptides that bound Qa-1 were identified. Following immunization with the identified HTNV peptides and subsequent HTNV challenge, wild-type (WT) mice showed attenuated renal immunopathology, whereas D227K knock-in mice (with disrupted Qa-1-CD8/TCR interaction) showed enhanced viral clearance in the spleen and kidney but exacerbated renal immunopathology. Mechanistically, Qa-1-restricted CD8 + Tregs from WT mice suppressed effector CD8 + T cell proliferation in a peptide-specific, CD8/TCR-dependent manner via enhanced TGF-β secretion. Strikingly, D227K mutation dichotomously reshaped Treg phenotype: bulk polyclonal CD8 + Tregs displayed compensatory upregulation of inhibitory receptors (NKG2A, CTLA-4, PD-1) and TGF-β, whereas epitope-specific CD8 + Tregs showed impaired antigen-specific suppressive function and attenuated TGF-β production. Collectively, these findings indicate that HLA-E/Qa-1-restricted CD8 + Tregs can restrain immunopathology during HTNV infection, potentially at the cost of delayed viral elimination. Modulation of this axis may provide insights for therapeutic strategies in HFRS and related viral hemorrhagic fevers.

articles_hidden.title: Transcranial magnetic stimulation to the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex modulates single-neuron activity in humans
articles_hidden.authors: Charles W. Dickey, Umair Hassan, Hiroto Kawasaki, Ariane E. Rhone, Christopher C. Cline, Matthew A. Howard, Nicholas T. Trapp, Aaron D. Boes, Joel I. Berger, Corey J. Keller
articles_hidden.abstract: Transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) to the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (dlPFC) is an established treatment for depression, yet the fundamental question of how cortical stimulation influences single neurons in deep brain circuits critical for mood regulation remains unanswered. Using a rare opportunity to record from intracranial microelectrodes while TMS was delivered in four neurosurgical patients, we evaluated the responses of 185 single neurons. Artifact cleaning enabled single-neuron spikes to be resolved as early as 8 ms after stimulation. We found that single-pulse TMS to the left dlPFC elicited time-locked firing responses in 46% of neurons (26% facilitated only, 19% suppressed only, 1% both). These responses occurred within deep bilateral cortical and subcortical structures, including the putamen and thalamus. Single-pulse TMS tended to facilitate spiking in striato-thalamic putative inhibitory neurons from ~8 ms, peaking at ~80 to 100 ms, and decaying until ~600 ms. In contrast, putative excitatory neurons and limbic areas were suppressed with a slower time course lasting to ~1,000 ms. TMS-evoked potentials recorded from intracranial depth macroelectrodes to quantify network activity revealed that the modulation of responsive neurons was positively correlated with cortico-striato-thalamic network activity and anticorrelated with limbic network activity in one participant with sufficient network and unit sampling. These results suggest that dlPFC TMS recruits a high percentage of neurons spanning cortical and subcortical brain regions bilaterally. The recruitment pattern selectively involves increasing the firing rate of inhibitory neurons in executive control networks while suppressing limbic excitatory drive, providing a candidate cellular mechanism for how cortical stimulation modulates distributed brain networks.

articles_hidden.title: Coacervate droplets as a liquefier for the solid-to-liquid transition of RNA aggregates
articles_hidden.authors: Wei Guo, Rong Luo, Yi Shen, Xiangze Zeng, Zhou Liu, Ho Cheung Shum
articles_hidden.abstract: Biomolecular condensates are functionally gated by their material properties. While RNA is a primary structural scaffold, its sequence-specific interactions can aberrantly drive condensates into dysfunctional solid aggregates. Yet, actively reversing this solidification to restore function remains a fundamental challenge, impeding progress in synthetic biology and therapeutics interventions. Here, we establish that complex coacervates can be engineered as liquefiers to actively remodel solid RNA–peptide aggregates into functional liquid droplets. Integrating systematic experiments with all-atom simulations, we decode a multiscale mechanism: coacervate infiltration at the micrometer scale mediates molecular buffering at the nanometer scale, which fluidizes the crosslinked network to drive macroscopic liquefaction. This capability is governed by a design rule, where coacervates formed by small-molecular anions exhibit optimal efficacy. We deploy this principle to functionally rescue silenced RNA within a model of pathologically solidified ribonucleoprotein assemblies. Our work provides a general framework for the active, compositional control of biomolecular phase behavior, with direct implications for managing pathological aggregation and engineering functional condensates in synthetic and living systems.

articles_hidden.title: Rising cell-free DNA level tracks cancer-associated methylation signal and improves multicancer detection
articles_hidden.authors: Swaraj Basu, Prakash Hiremath, Nihesh Rathod, Aditi Chatterjee, Divya Vishwanath, Arunima Ghosh, T. Sthanusubramonian, Shashank Kumar, Krithika Subramanian, Preetha R. T., Arya Nair, Kannadhasan Sekar, Sarath R. A., Subuhi Yete, Bhanumathy G., Urvashi Bahadur, Aneesha Radhakrishnan, Abhishek Sarkar, Siddikuzzaman, Alfiya Beig, Ankita Khan, Badri Padhukasahasram, Lavanya Nemani, Lavanya Bollipalli, Pallavi Ghana, Sameer Phalke, Sewanti Limaye, Vijay Chandru, Vamsi Veeramachaneni, Ramesh Hariharan, Charles R. Cantor
articles_hidden.abstract: Cancer patients carry more circulating cell-free DNA (ccfDNA)—small DNA fragments shed into the blood—than healthy people. Most of this excess comes not from the tumor itself but from immune cells, suggesting that it would simply dilute the much smaller amount of tumor-derived DNA in a blood sample. Using a study of 1,480 previously untreated participants across 43 hospitals—including patients with 14 cancer types spanning all stages, patients with benign growths, and healthy volunteers—we show the opposite: as total ccfDNA rises, it becomes enriched, not diluted, in fragments carrying cancer-associated DNA methylation signatures, independent of cancer type, disease stage, and a broad panel of demographic, clinical, and technical covariates. In fact, total ccfDNA explains more variance in cancer-associated methylation signal than the disease stage itself. This basic biological finding suggests a coupling between immune cell activity and tumor methylation. It also has a practical implication: we show that rising ccfDNA concentration is associated with higher cancer detection sensitivity, even within disease stages and particularly in early-stage disease—stage I sensitivity varied from 0.55 in the lowest ccfDNA concentration tertile to 0.85 in the highest, and stage II from 0.59 to 0.86. This suggests that ccfDNA concentration should be considered as a stage-independent stratification variable for benchmarking cancer-detection tests. Interestingly, similar behavior was observed in patients with symptomatic benign lesions, suggesting a broader biological response to abnormal tissue growth and not something unique to malignancy.

articles_hidden.title: Modified Newtonian Dynamics and galaxy clusters
articles_hidden.authors: Francoise Combes
articles_hidden.abstract: First proposed by Milgrom in 1983 as an alternative to the standard Cold Dark Matter (CDM) paradigm, Modified Newtonian Dynamics (MOND) has gained renewed momentum in light of persistent nondetections of exotic dark matter particles and growing tensions facing CDM on galactic scales. While MOND perfectly reproduces galactic rotation curves, it encounters notable challenges in explaining the equilibrium of galaxy clusters. Although it reduces the overall dark matter budget in these massive systems, an unidentified mass component remains required. This paper investigates the hypothesis that this missing mass is baryonic: composed of nonradiating ordinary matter such as stellar remnants, gas too diffuse to initiate star formation, or compact, ultra-dense clouds of cold molecular gas with low volume filling factors. Using a sample of 106 clusters mapped in X-rays, emitted by the hot intracluster medium composing most of the visible mass, we derive first the total mass within the Newtonian dynamics, assuming hydrostatic equilibrium and spherical symmetry. Then, with the modified Poisson equation, we reconstruct the spatial distribution of the invisible missing matter within the MOND framework. In the sample, the relaxed systems harboring cooling flows, known as cool-core clusters, have the highest peaks of dark missing mass. Its density profile reveals a pronounced central concentration bounded by a steep truncation immediately beyond a core radius of 20 to 30 kpc, confirming previous studies. MOND reduces the necessary dynamical mass by a factor of 4 to 10. The residual missing mass is proportional to the total gas mass, being roughly twice lower.

articles_hidden.title: Comprehensive classification of HCN1 variants linked to neurodevelopmental disorders with and without epilepsy
articles_hidden.authors: Roberta Castelli, Carla Marini, Alessandro Porro, Anna Castellini, Greta Fontana, Andrea Saponaro, Gianpiero L. Cavalleri, Susanna Rizzi, Carlo Fusco, Amitav Parida, Richard Caswell, Charlotte Sherlaw-Sturrock, Dario Pruna, Christopher A. Reid, Lauren E. Bleakley, Katherine B. Howell, Ingrid E. Scheffer, Vishnu Anand Cuddapah, Shimriet Zeidler, Elena Pavlidis, Deb K. Pal, Krzysztof Szczałuba, Ghayda Mirzaa, Nathalie Couque, Yline Capri, Laurence Faivre, Frederic Tran Mau-Them, Fabio Sirchia, Christian M. Korff, Dario DiFrancesco, Gerhard Thiel, Christel Depienne, Bina Santoro, Anna Moroni
articles_hidden.abstract: Hyperpolarization-activated cyclic nucleotide-gated 1 (HCN1) channels mediate the cationic I h current, a fundamental regulator of neuronal excitability and synaptic integration, and are predominantly expressed in the cortex and hippocampus. Although HCN1 variants have been increasingly identified in patients with epilepsy, from milder forms to developmental and epileptic encephalopathies (DEE), genotype–phenotype correlations remain poorly defined. Here, we used patch-clamp electrophysiology and confocal imaging in HEK293 cells to functionally characterize 43 HCN1 variants identified in patients with neurodevelopmental disorders, with or without epilepsy. Based on biophysical properties, we established a classification system comprising four distinct functional classes: I) low or no current; II) hyperpolarizing shift in voltage dependence; III) depolarizing shift in voltage dependence; and IV) generation of an instantaneous current. The molecular basis for this classification was further interpreted using available cryo-EM structures of HCN1. Integration with clinical data from 50 patients revealed a striking correlation between functional class and clinical presentation. Loss-of-function variants prevailed among individuals with milder phenotypes or without epilepsy, with the latter distinctively clustering within the channel selectivity filter. In contrast, gain-of-function and mixed variants were predominantly associated with DEE. Finally, we demonstrate that allosteric modulators, including peptides NB6 and TRIP8b nano and the small molecule J&J12e, effectively normalize channel function across three of the four classes in vitro. These findings establish a biophysical framework for interpreting HCN1 variants, demonstrating that the direction of channel dysfunction is a major determinant of epilepsy risk and severity, and providing a conceptual foundation for future class-based precision medicine approaches.

articles_hidden.title: Geochemical signatures of magnetite are conserved in diverse populations of environmental magnetotactic bacteria
articles_hidden.authors: Vincent Busigny, Akanksha Praharaj, Matthieu Amor, François P. Mathon, Caroline L. Monteil, Nicolas Menguy, Karim Benzerara, Neha Mehta, Didier Jézéquel, Eric Viollier, Christopher T. Lefèvre
articles_hidden.abstract: Magnetotactic bacteria (MTB) synthesize intracellular magnetite nanoparticles in a genetically controlled manner. They may represent some of the earliest biomineralizing organisms on Earth, and a unique window into ancient life and the environments that hosted it. Yet, identification of their mineralogical remains in ancient rocks is highly challenging due to the lack of reliable and lasting proxies. Previous results obtained from laboratory cultures of single strains of MTB revealed trace element and Fe isotope patterns that are not shared by any other source of magnetite, which could be used as reliable proxies for the identification of ancient MTB. However, the environmental relevance of these previous findings for environmental and mixed population of MTB is unknown. We report the trace element and Fe isotope compositions of magnetite extracted from environmental MTB collected in the water column of Lake Pavin, France, and show that the most distinctive geochemical traits (enrichment in Mo, Se, Sn, and light Fe isotopes) of magnetite produced by MTB cultivated in the laboratory are conserved in environmental populations. They represent potential biological signatures that can be searched in ancient rocks and coupled with magnetic and mineralogical tracers to support the presence of MTB and reconstruct their emergence and evolution.

articles_hidden.title: Molecular basis of quorum-sensing signal transduction by CqsS and its inhibition by CqsA, the autoinducer synthase
articles_hidden.authors: Mengchan Liu, Yufan Yang, Julie S. Valastyan, Yuru Zhang, Grace A. Beggs, Yanhong Liu, Zhenhua Wang, Bonnie L. Bassler, Hongwu Qian
articles_hidden.abstract: Vibrio bacteria possess multiple quorum-sensing systems, each of which conveys information into the cell concerning the cell density and species composition of the vicinal community. Germane to the present work is the CqsA-CqsS quorum-sensing pathway that vibrios use for intragenus communication. CqsA is the synthase for the autoinducer ( S )-3-hydroxytridecan-4-one (CAI-1), and CqsS, a bifunctional two-component kinase-phosphatase, is the CAI-1 receptor. Here, we determine the cryo-EM structures of the full-length Vibrio harveyi CqsS dimer in the apo- and ATPγS-bound states. Our structures reveal the molecular basis for the initiation of the phosphorylation cascade, which we support through biochemical and genetic analyses. Autophosphorylation of CqsS occurs in cis at the conserved histidine residue (H1), whereas phospho-transfer to the conserved aspartate residue (D1) in the C-terminal receiver domain occurs in trans . By coexpressing CqsS and CqsA to capture CqsS bound to CAI-1, we unexpectedly find a tight interaction between the CqsS intracellular domain and CqsA. In the complex, the CqsS H1 residues are positioned away from the catalytic cavity, and CqsS kinase activity is inhibited. Cryo-EM analysis, focused on the transmembrane domain of CqsS in this complex, reveals the presence of two CAI-1 molecules. CAI-1 binding induces an obvious movement of transmembrane helix 6, disrupting its extension into the cytosol, providing a structural basis for how CAI-1 binding in the periplasm is coupled to signal transduction into the cytoplasm. Together, our findings advance the understanding of CqsS-CAI-1-mediated quorum-sensing signal transduction, an activity that underpins the coordination of group behaviors in vibrios.

articles_hidden.title: Hypothalamic lncRNA Synage prevents age-related sperm quality decline by suppressing A-type potassium currents in GnRH neurons
articles_hidden.authors: Fei Wang, Mengyi Zhang, Mengtian Wang, Shuhan Tian, Qian Bian, Yaohui He, Shuiqiao Yuan, Qinghua Shi, Wen Liu, Jun Xiao, Li Wang, Ji Liu, Xiaoyuan Song
articles_hidden.abstract: Age-related decline in male fertility, including diminished sperm quality, poses significant risks to offspring health and is exacerbated by modern trends toward delayed parenthood. Focusing on the hypothalamus–pituitary–testis axis, which governs hormonal control of male reproduction, we identified Synage , a long noncoding RNA expressed in the hypothalamic medial preoptic area (mPOA). We found that Synage expression in gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH) neurons decreases with age, correlating with reduced sperm quality and male fertility. mPOA-targeted Synage _B (brain-specific isoform) supplementation increases serum testosterone and improves sperm count and progressive motility in 12-mo-old mice. Conversely, conditional deletion of Synage in GnRH neurons in young mice reduces GnRH neuron firing, decreases serum LH and testosterone levels, impaires sperm quality, and reduces male fertility. Mechanistically, Synage interacts with the heat shock protein HSPA8 and stabilizes the HSPA8–KCHIP4 interaction. Synage loss increases KCHIP4 abundance and its association with the Kv4.2 channel, promoting Kv4.2 membrane recruitment and enhancing A-type potassium currents ( I A ), thereby reducing GnRH neuronal excitability. Consistent with this model, GnRH neurons from 12-mo-old mice also exhibit reduced excitability. Together, these findings support a role for age-dependent Synage loss in reproductive decline, at least in part through dysregulation of the HSPA8–KCHIP4–Kv4.2 pathway and reduced GnRH neuron excitability. These findings identify Synage as a candidate regulator of reproductive aging and motivate further investigation of its translational potential.

articles_hidden.title: Spontaneous gas film expansion at an oil–water interface
articles_hidden.authors: Bowen Zhang, Jinlong Yang, Shiji Lin, Yue Fan, Junchang Guo, Boru Wei, Yuhao Hu, Yang Shen, Shuqi Zhang, Guanyu Zhou, Longquan Chen, Xu Deng
articles_hidden.abstract: Spontaneous interfacial separation of oil and water, by inserting a gas film between the two liquids, is thermodynamically unfavorable because the oil–water interface is replaced by oil–gas and water–gas interfaces with a higher combined interfacial energy. Here, we demonstrate that microstructural confinement enables this transition after bubble introduction through the coupling of wetting, capillarity, and gas transport. Spontaneous oil imbibition into a water-submerged micropillar array, together with local contact-line pinning, deforms the oil–water interface into a metastable meniscus and generates a local pressure deficit in the confined oil. This deficit, combined with the bubble’s interfacial configuration, lowers its air partial pressure and promotes dissolved-air uptake from the surrounding water. Geometric confinement, reduced oil pressure, and low oil–gas interfacial tension favor bubble lateral invasion of adjacent oil-filled cells over vertical extrusion. As the gas front advances, meniscus relaxation and oil redistribution promote further wetting, renewing the capillary conditions that support gas film propagation. We develop a coupled transport-capillarity framework that captures these morphological transitions and predicts a characteristic timescale for gas film evolution, determined by the interaction among geometry, capillarity, and gas-phase transport. Spatially varying the microstructure further controls the propagation pathway and morphology of the gas film. These findings show how favorable wetting can support an energetically costly interfacial transformation through a confinement-induced capillary pressure field, providing a general mechanism for gas-mediated separation in confined multiphase systems.

articles_hidden.title: Multifunctional multiphysics metamaterials via decomposition-based multiobjective optimization design
articles_hidden.authors: Zhuo Chen, Sha Yin, Zihao Zhu, Yuehua Liu, Jiping Yang, Robert O. Ritchie, Yiu Wing Mai
articles_hidden.abstract: Metamaterials offer unprecedented control over physical fields through their microstructure, but current design methods cannot meet the demands of scenarios involving active sources, multiphysics field coupling, and multifunctional requirements. Moreover, existing approaches are generally developed for specific functions, making it difficult to integrate different functionalities and select the functional priorities within a single structure. To overcome these limitations, this study presents a systematic inverse design framework for multifunctional multiphysics metamaterials via multiobjective optimization. To uniformly explore the Pareto front, which clearly exhibits trade-offs among functionalities and facilitates the selection of functional priorities, we employ dynamic normalization into the decomposition-based multiobjective evolutionary algorithm. A robust anisotropic unit-cell database is constructed and used for generating metamaterials with optimized microstructures for multifunctionality. Three complex cases are studied that can simultaneously achieve mechanical cloaking plus stress minimization, thermal cloaking plus stress minimization, and direct current cloaking plus thermal stress minimization. Furthermore, the proposed framework is employed in potential engineering problems, for example, to realize mechanical cloaking by embedding functional components in structural materials, while minimizing the surrounding stress on functional components for mechanical protection when the assembled structures are compressed, thereby decoupling the interaction between functional and structural components. This systematic framework expands the capabilities of metamaterials in complex multiphysics coupling, offering a robust blueprint for future intelligent, structurally and functionally integrated systems.

articles_hidden.title: Progressive shifts in soil respiration response to long-term nitrogen enrichment across global forests and grasslands
articles_hidden.authors: Aijun Xing, Mengying Zhao, Shangshi Liu, Arthur A. D. Broadbent, Enzai Du, Haihua Shen, Jingyun Fang
articles_hidden.abstract: Soil stores the largest pool of actively cycling carbon (C) on land, and its dynamics under global changes are critical for projecting climate feedbacks. Global nitrogen (N) deposition has more than doubled since the 1860s; however, the temporal dynamics of soil C emissions under prolonged N deposition are poorly understood. Here, using a global time-series dataset compiled from 38 long-term experiments in forests and grasslands, we find that the response of soil respiration (Rs) to N addition systematically shifts from a transient increase persisting for approximately 2 y to a sustained suppression over time (mean effect = −6%; 95% CI = [−10%, −3%]). Rs in forests and grasslands followed consistent nonlinear trajectories, characterized by a rapid initial decline in the magnitude of the response, which progressively leveled off. Notably, suppression of Rs emerged when cumulative N inputs exceeded a threshold of ~100 kg N ha −1 . Consequently, the suppression was both stronger and occurred more rapidly under high-level N additions (>50 kg N ha −1 y −1 ). These temporal dynamics were associated with N-induced soil acidification and related changes in microbial properties. Overall, these findings indicate that accurate prediction of land–atmosphere C fluxes under global change requires models to capture the reported temporal dynamics.
